The last lighthouse keepers of the northern coast

Words by Tomasz Lindqvist

For eleven years Agnes Fairweather climbed one hundred and twelve steps every evening to light the lamp at Corran Point, and every morning she climbed them again to put it out. She is one of only four people still alive who kept a lighthouse on this stretch of coast before the lights were automated.

The work was less romantic than people imagine, she says. There were brass fittings to polish, a log to keep in a neat hand, a fog signal to wind by hand when the weather closed in, and long winters when the supply boat could not land for weeks at a time.

What she remembers most is the silence. When the lamp turned, the only sound was the clockwork, a slow tick that she could hear through the floor of the kitchen two storeys below. Visitors would ask whether it drove her mad. It did the opposite: she slept badly for a year after she left.

The keepers' cottages at Corran Point now house a small museum, run by volunteers, with the original log books on display. The entries are mostly about the weather, but between the barometer readings there are notes about seals on the rocks, a wedding in the village, and a ship that passed too close one night in March 1979.

Fairweather visits twice a year. She no longer climbs to the lamp room, but she still checks that the brass on the front door has been polished.
